Descriptions.Explanation:
Certain functions behave in dangerous or unexpected ways. Functions in this category were often implemented without taking security concerns into account. In this case, the dangerous function you are using is in on line . The Mysql.escape_string() and Mysql.quote() functions should not be relied upon for securing objects going into a dynamically created SQL query. Example 1: The following code shows why it is dangerous to rely upon these functions for escaping user input going into a dynamically created SQL query. 
...
id = Mysql.escape_string(params[:id])
password = Mysql.escape_string(params[:password])
query = "SELECT * FROM USERS WHERE id=#{id} AND password='#{password}'"
result = conn.query(query)
...
In this example if an attacker tried manipulating the password parameter by entering an apostrophe, Mysql.escape_string() will escape this as \', stopping the query from breaking. However, due to Ruby being a dynamically typed language, even though the query is expecting an integer of some variant, id can be any type. If an attacker modified the id parameter to be 1#, this would modify the SQL query into: "SELECT * FROM USERS WHERE id=1# AND password='anyPassword'" As MySQL treats # as the start of a comment, this means that the query will simply search for user where id=1, effectively getting around the password authentication.

Certain functions behave in dangerous ways. Functions in this category were often implemented without taking security concerns into account. In this case, the dangerous function you are using is in on line . The Mysql2::Client#escape() function should not be relied upon for securing objects going into a dynamically created SQL query. Example 1: The following code shows why it is dangerous to rely upon these functions for escaping user input going into a dynamically created SQL query. 
...
id = Mysql2::Client.escape(params[:id])
password = Mysql2::Client.escape(params[:password])
query = "SELECT * FROM USERS WHERE id=#{id} AND password='#{password}'"
result = client.query(query)
...
In this example if an attacker tried manipulating the password parameter by entering an apostrophe, Mysql2::Client.escape() will escape this as \', stopping the query from breaking. However, due to Ruby being a dynamically typed language, even though the query is expecting an integer of some variant, id can be any type. If an attacker modified the id parameter to be 1#, this would modify the SQL query into: "SELECT * FROM USERS WHERE id=1# AND password='anyPassword'" As MySQL treats # as the start of a comment, this means that the query will simply search for user where id=1, effectively getting around the password authentication.

MD2, MD4, MD5, RIPEMD-160, and SHA-1 are popular cryptographic hash algorithms often used to verify the integrity of messages and other data. Recent advances in cryptanalysis have discovered weaknesses in these algorithms. Consequently, they should no longer be relied upon to verify the authenticity of data in security-critical contexts. Techniques for breaking MD and RIPEMD hashes are advanced and widely available enough that the algorithms must not be relied upon for security. In the case of SHA-1, current techniques still require a significant amount of computational power and are more difficult to implement. However, attackers have found the Achilles' heel for the algorithm, and techniques for breaking it will likely lead to the discovery of even faster attacks. The String#crypt function depends on the standard library function crypt on the current platform. Even when specifying the hash type to be used, this may depend on platform, implementation, and versions of libraries available to the user running the application.

Certain functions behave in dangerous ways regardless of how they are used. Functions in this category were often implemented without taking security concerns into account. In this case, the dangerous function you are using is in on line . The PG::Connection#escape_bytea() function is unsafe as it calls PQescapeString() or PQescapeBytea() in the background, which do not take into consideration the current character encoding set within the database. Thus, it may be vulnerable to multi-byte escaping issues. The validation performed by PG::Connection#escape_bytea also does not work for values that are supposed to be numeric, as the object could be any type due to Ruby not being statically typed, and thus would require additional checks to verify the type of the object.

Certain functions behave in dangerous or unexpected ways. Functions in this category were often implemented without taking security concerns into account. In this case, the dangerous function you are using is in on line . The PG::Connection#escape_string() and PG::Connection#escape_bytea() functions should not be relied upon for securing objects going into a dynamically created SQL query as they do not allow for null bytes which could cause SQL Injection via truncation using null bytes. Example 1: The following code shows why it is dangerous to rely upon these functions for escaping user input going into a dynamically created SQL query. 
...
query = conn.escape_string("SELECT * FROM users WHERE age < #{user_input} AND salary > 100000")
res = conn.exec(query)
...
The attacker could change user_input to "25 or 1<5\x00" which would then cause the query to be truncated to: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE age < 25 or 1<5". Since "1<5" always evaluates to true, this will mean all records from the users table will be returned to res. However, even if there existed an additional check prior to this to verify user_input did not contain null bytes, it would not prevent additional checks being specified within the SQL query, as this only protects against string values.
Descriptions.Recommendations: Refrain from using functions that behave in unexpected or dangerous ways. Ideally these should be removed from all code and replaced with safer alternatives. If necessary where they can potentially be used in safe ways, all uses should be closely audited in order to make sure no nefarious actions may follow. The Mysql library has functionality for parameterized SQL statements, which should always be used instead of dynamically creating SQL queries. The Mysql.escape_string() and Mysql.quote() functions should not be relied upon for securing SQL queries against SQL injection.

Refrain from using functions that behave in unexpected or dangerous ways. Ideally these should be removed from all code and replaced with safer alternatives. If necessary where they can potentially be used in safe ways, all uses should be closely audited in order to make sure no nefarious actions may follow. The Mysql2 library does not currently have functionality for parameterized SQL statements, which should always be used instead of dynamically creating SQL queries. Therefore we suggest using an alternative library that has this functionality. The Mysql2::Client.escape() function should not be relied upon for securing SQL queries against SQL injection. However, if using this library is the only option then further validation should be performed to only accept a certain subset of characters that are deemed safe, and all others should either be rejected or modified to be safe.

Functions that cannot be used safely should never be used. If any of these functions occur in new or legacy code, they must be removed and replaced with safe alternatives. calls a backend function which has been deprecated and should not be used. Instead of using this function, parameterized queries should be used to ensure SQL injection is not possible. Example 1: When connecting to a PostgreSQL database, it is safer and more maintainable to use parameterized SQL statements (instead of concatenating user supplied strings via an escaping function) as follows: 
require 'pg'
...
begin
  ...
  req = Rack::Request.new(env) #gets GET and POST parameters from connection
  conn = PG::Connection.new(connection_hash) #uses a hash including all the relevant connection options
  query = "SELECT * FROM iterms WHERE owner=$1 and itemname=$2"
  ...
  params = [req.params['owner'], req.params['itemname']]
  conn.exec_params(query, params) do |result|
    ...
  end
rescue PG::ConnectionBad
  ...
...
ensure
  ...
end
